passage:
Most bird species raise their young in a simple arrangement: a breeding pair attends a single brood, and older offspring disperse at the end of their first season to seek territories of their own. In a smaller but well-documented set of species, however, this pattern is replaced by what biologists call cooperative breeding. In cooperatively breeding species, some adult offspring postpone their own reproduction and remain on their parents' territory for an extended period as nonbreeding helpers, assisting in feeding nestlings, defending the territory against intruders, or standing guard against predators.

Three conditions, taken together, appear to favor the evolution of this arrangement. First, suitable territories must be scarce enough that a young adult's chance of successfully establishing a new territory in a given year is low. Second, the habitat must be stable enough from year to year that waiting on a parental territory is not simply a wasted season; if conditions shift rapidly, the value of remaining at home collapses. Third, the presence of additional helpers must measurably increase the survival of the nestlings they assist, so that a helper contributes, indirectly, to the propagation of genes it shares with its siblings.

Where all three conditions hold, cooperative breeding is observed with some regularity; where any one of them is clearly absent, the arrangement is rare or absent as well. Researchers therefore describe cooperative breeding not as a puzzle requiring a distinct explanation for each species but as a predictable response to a recurring ecological situation, one in which waiting and helping together yield more inclusive fitness than early dispersal would.
comparativeBPassage:
The Florida scrub-jay, a bird confined to a narrow band of well-drained oak scrub on the Florida peninsula, provides an unusually clear illustration of cooperative breeding. Scrub-jay territories are defined by small patches of suitable scrub, and new patches rarely open up: roughly a third of adult scrub-jays spend a year or more as nonbreeders, waiting for a territory to become available through the death of a resident or the gradual expansion of their parents' range. The habitat itself is remarkably stable, with the same oak patches persisting across generations of jays and with the vegetation recovering in predictable ways after periodic fires.

During the nonbreeding period, most such birds live on their parents' territory and act as helpers. A helper's duties include feeding nestlings, escorting fledglings on their first flights, and, most notably, maintaining a sentinel position on a high perch from which approaching hawks and snakes can be spotted and announced to the group with a loud alarm call. Long-term studies at the Archbold Biological Station have shown that nests with helpers fledge measurably more young than nests without helpers, and that the helpers are almost always older offspring of the breeding pair rather than unrelated birds from neighboring territories.

The species thus displays each element one would expect to find in a cooperative breeder: a short supply of territories, a habitat that rewards waiting, and a clear fitness benefit to the helper's close relatives. For researchers, the scrub-jay has become a standard reference case against which other candidate cooperative breeders are compared.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Passage A defends a general account that passage B shows to be mistaken in the case of one species.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage A sets out a general account of cooperative breeding in birds, and passage B describes a single species that exhibits each of the features the general account identifies.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passage A and passage B offer competing explanations for the behavior of the Florida scrub-jay.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passage A describes a controversy among biologists that passage B resolves in favor of one side.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage A surveys a range of bird species, and passage B argues that cooperative breeding has been overreported in the literature.

explanations.correct: Passage A lays out the three conditions that favor cooperative breeding in general; passage B describes the Florida scrub-jay as a species in which each of those three conditions is satisfied. That is a generalization/instance relationship.
explanations.A: Passage B does not argue that the general account is mistaken; it presents the scrub-jay as a case that fits the account.
explanations.C: The two passages do not offer competing explanations; only passage B discusses the scrub-jay, and it uses the framework of passage A.
explanations.D: Passage A does not describe a controversy.
explanations.E: Passage B does not claim that cooperative breeding has been overreported; it presents the scrub-jay as a standard reference case.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of passage A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cooperative breeding is a puzzle that requires a separate evolutionary explanation for each species in which it occurs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most bird species raise their young in breeding pairs rather than in cooperative groups.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cooperative breeding in birds is best understood as a predictable response to three specifiable ecological conditions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Young adult birds generally benefit more from remaining on their parents' territory than from seeking territories of their own.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Helpers at the nest increase the survival of their siblings only when suitable territories are scarce.

explanations.correct: The third paragraph states the passage's main claim explicitly: cooperative breeding is not a puzzle requiring a distinct explanation for each species but a predictable response to a recurring ecological situation, namely the three conditions laid out in paragraph 2.
explanations.A: The passage's final paragraph rejects this framing.
explanations.B: This is a framing claim from paragraph 1, not the passage's thesis.
explanations.D: The passage does not claim this; helpers forgo reproduction during the waiting period.
explanations.E: The passage treats scarcity of territories and survival benefit as separate conditions, both of which must hold.

questions.questionStem: According to passage A, each of the following is a condition that favors the evolution of cooperative breeding EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: the scarcity of suitable territories for young adult birds

choices.label: B
choices.text: year-to-year stability of the relevant habitat

choices.label: C
choices.text: a measurable increase in nestling survival when helpers are present

choices.label: D
choices.text: a low average reproductive rate among the breeding pairs of the species

choices.label: E
choices.text: a genetic relationship between helpers and the nestlings they assist

explanations.correct: Passage A lists exactly three conditions: scarce territories, stable habitat, and a survival benefit from helpers that operates through shared genes. The passage does not mention low reproductive rate as a precondition.
explanations.A: This is the first condition stated.
explanations.B: This is the second condition stated.
explanations.C: This is the third condition stated.
explanations.D: Correct. The passage does not name this as a condition.
explanations.E: Passage A's third condition explicitly depends on the helper sharing genes with its siblings.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following is mentioned in passage B but not in passage A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: that helpers assist in feeding nestlings

choices.label: B
choices.text: that helpers contribute indirectly to the propagation of shared genes

choices.label: C
choices.text: that helpers may take up a sentinel position from which approaching predators can be spotted

choices.label: D
choices.text: that cooperative breeding is observed in only a smaller subset of bird species

choices.label: E
choices.text: that the habitat of a cooperatively breeding species must be relatively stable from year to year

explanations.correct: Passage B states that a helper's duties include 'maintaining a sentinel position on a high perch from which approaching hawks and snakes can be spotted and announced to the group.' Passage A mentions feeding, territory defense, and guarding against predators in general terms but does not describe a sentinel perch.
explanations.B: Passage A makes this point explicitly about shared genes; passage B mentions a fitness benefit to close relatives but does not introduce this idea for the first time.
explanations.D: Only passage A frames the relative frequency of the arrangement.
explanations.E: Passage A identifies habitat stability as one of the three conditions.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following features of the Florida scrub-jay, as described in passage B, most directly corresponds to the first of the three conditions identified in passage A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the tendency of helpers to be older offspring of the breeding pair

choices.label: B
choices.text: the fact that roughly a third of adult scrub-jays spend a year or more as nonbreeders waiting for a territory

choices.label: C
choices.text: the persistence of the same oak patches across generations of jays

choices.label: D
choices.text: the finding that nests with helpers fledge measurably more young than nests without

choices.label: E
choices.text: the use of the species as a standard reference case by researchers

explanations.correct: Passage A's first condition is that suitable territories must be scarce enough that a young adult's chance of establishing a new territory in a given year is low. Passage B's report that roughly a third of adult scrub-jays spend a year or more waiting for a territory is the direct instantiation of that scarcity.
explanations.A: This fact corresponds to the genetic-relatedness element of the third condition, not the scarcity condition.
explanations.C: Persistent oak patches correspond to the second condition (stable habitat), not the first.
explanations.D: This corresponds to the third condition (survival benefit from helpers).
explanations.E: This describes how other researchers use the species, not any of passage A's three conditions.

questions.questionStem: The passages most strongly support which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cooperative breeding is more common among birds than the breeding-pair arrangement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most adult Florida scrub-jays never succeed in establishing territories of their own.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A bird species whose habitat changes dramatically from year to year is unlikely to develop cooperative breeding.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cooperative breeding in the Florida scrub-jay evolved independently of cooperative breeding in other species.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Helpers in cooperatively breeding species contribute more to nestling survival than the breeding pair does.

explanations.correct: Passage A identifies year-to-year habitat stability as a necessary condition; where a condition 'is clearly absent, the arrangement is rare or absent as well.' A species whose habitat changes dramatically from year to year therefore lacks that condition and is unlikely to develop cooperative breeding.
explanations.A: Passage A explicitly identifies cooperative breeding as the less common arrangement.
explanations.B: Passage B says roughly a third of adults spend a year or more waiting, not that most never establish territories.
explanations.D: Neither passage addresses the independent origins of cooperative breeding in different lineages.
explanations.E: Neither passage compares the contribution of helpers with that of breeding pairs.

questions.questionStem: In passage B, the reference to long-term studies at the Archbold Biological Station functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: cast doubt on the general account of cooperative breeding presented in passage A

choices.label: B
choices.text: provide evidence that helpers in the Florida scrub-jay increase the survival of nestlings to which they are closely related

choices.label: C
choices.text: identify the researchers who first proposed the three-condition framework described in passage A

choices.label: D
choices.text: illustrate the difficulty of observing cooperative breeding in stable habitats

choices.label: E
choices.text: introduce a rival species whose behavior does not fit passage A's framework

explanations.correct: The Archbold sentence reports two findings: that nests with helpers fledge more young, and that helpers are almost always older offspring of the breeding pair. Together these support the instantiation of passage A's third condition — a fitness benefit that runs through close relatives.
explanations.A: The studies are used to support, not undermine, the general account.
explanations.C: Passage B does not attribute the three-condition framework to any particular researchers.
explanations.D: The studies do not illustrate any difficulty of observation.
explanations.E: No rival species is introduced; the scrub-jay is the sole focus of passage B.

passage:
Historians of public health have sometimes argued that epidemics rarely introduce entirely new social trends; more often, they accelerate developments that were already under way before the outbreak began. On this view, a severe outbreak acts less as an engine of change than as a pressure that shortens the time required for existing proposals — proposals that had been circulating among reformers and officials well in advance of the crisis — to be adopted in practice.

Three features of this accelerating role tend to recur. First, the institutional proposals that an epidemic advances are typically those already in reasonably developed form when the epidemic arrives; the crisis rewards readiness rather than improvisation, and ideas that had not yet been articulated before the outbreak rarely enter the official record during it. Second, the acceleration is most pronounced in domains where the proposed changes had already begun to attract some official support, even if adoption had been delayed by competing priorities or local resistance. Third, once the emergency recedes, the newly adopted arrangements usually persist, because dismantling them would require actively reversing changes that were already on a path toward acceptance.

By treating epidemics as accelerants rather than as originators, historians can explain why outwardly similar outbreaks in different societies often produce sharply different institutional outcomes: the outcome reflects what was already available to be accelerated. This framing avoids the temptation to treat every post-epidemic reform as a direct consequence of the epidemic itself and focuses attention instead on the preexisting trajectory that the crisis intensified.
comparativeBPassage:
The 1918 influenza pandemic reached the United States at a moment when American public-health administration was in an unsettled condition. For more than a decade, progressive reformers had been urging the expansion of state and municipal health departments, the systematic collection of vital statistics, and the creation of standing advisory bodies to coordinate responses across jurisdictions. These proposals had generated official interest in a number of states, and pilot arrangements existed in several cities; but full adoption had been delayed by budget disputes and by resistance from local authorities who regarded public-health administration as a local rather than a state function.

The pandemic shifted this balance within a matter of months. Several states that had been considering the expansion of their health departments enacted the relevant legislation in 1919 and 1920, drawing largely on draft statutes that had been prepared before the outbreak. The systematic reporting of communicable disease — a longstanding reformer demand — was institutionalized in many jurisdictions during the same period. Coordinating bodies that had previously been proposed and shelved were established on a standing basis.

After the pandemic subsided, these arrangements remained in place. The health departments did not shrink back to their prewar size; the reporting requirements were not repealed; the coordinating bodies continued to meet. The episode is frequently cited as a clear instance of the pattern in which a crisis rapidly advances a program of reform that was already in circulation before the crisis arrived.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Passage A proposes a general principle about the historical role of epidemics, and passage B presents a specific episode that conforms to that principle.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage A describes a historical episode, and passage B draws from that episode a general principle about all crises.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passage A defends a principle that passage B argues is incompatible with the American historical record.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passage A and passage B offer competing accounts of the causes of the 1918 influenza pandemic.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage A surveys reforms in several countries, and passage B narrows that survey to the United States alone.

explanations.correct: Passage A sets out the 'accelerant' principle, with three recurring features. Passage B presents the 1918 influenza pandemic as an episode that displays each of those features. That is a principle/application relationship.
explanations.B: The order is reversed: passage A is general, passage B is specific.
explanations.C: Passage B is presented as an instance of passage A's principle, not a counterexample.
explanations.D: Neither passage discusses the biological or epidemiological causes of the pandemic.
explanations.E: Passage A does not survey reforms in particular countries.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of passage A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Epidemics usually introduce entirely new social trends that would not have emerged in their absence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Epidemics typically accelerate reforms that were already developing, rather than originating new ones, in ways that can be described by several recurring features.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Institutional reforms adopted during an epidemic are usually reversed once the emergency has passed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Outwardly similar epidemics in different societies generally produce similar institutional outcomes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reformers should not propose new public-health measures until an epidemic has already begun.

explanations.correct: Passage A argues that epidemics accelerate developments already under way and identifies three recurring features of this accelerating role.
explanations.A: Passage A explicitly rejects this view in its first paragraph.
explanations.C: Passage A says the opposite: the arrangements usually persist.
explanations.D: Passage A says outwardly similar outbreaks can produce sharply different outcomes.
explanations.E: Passage A makes no policy recommendation to reformers.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following questions is central to both passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: What role do epidemics play in shaping subsequent institutional arrangements?

choices.label: B
choices.text: What medical interventions proved most effective during the 1918 influenza pandemic?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Why did some early-twentieth-century municipalities resist state-level public-health administration?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Should reformers rely on crises to advance proposals that cannot be adopted in ordinary times?

choices.label: E
choices.text: How should historians weigh archival evidence against statistical records when studying epidemics?

explanations.correct: Passage A asks, and answers, this question in general terms (epidemics accelerate existing trends). Passage B addresses the same question in a specific case (the 1918 pandemic accelerated preexisting public-health proposals).
explanations.C: Passage B briefly notes municipal resistance but does not ask or answer this question; passage A does not touch it at all.
explanations.D: Neither passage frames the issue as a recommendation to reformers.

questions.questionStem: According to passage B, prior to the 1918 pandemic, full adoption of the reformers' public-health proposals had been delayed primarily by

choices.label: A
choices.text: the absence of any official interest in those proposals

choices.label: B
choices.text: a lack of draft legislation suitable for enactment

choices.label: C
choices.text: budget disputes and resistance from local authorities who regarded public-health administration as a local rather than a state function

choices.label: D
choices.text: the opposition of progressive reformers to centralization

choices.label: E
choices.text: a federal statute prohibiting the states from expanding their health departments

explanations.correct: Passage B states: 'full adoption had been delayed by budget disputes and by resistance from local authorities who regarded public-health administration as a local rather than a state function.'
explanations.A: The passage says the proposals had generated official interest in a number of states.
explanations.B: The passage says states drew on draft statutes that had been prepared before the outbreak.
explanations.D: Progressive reformers were the ones urging the changes.
explanations.E: The passage does not mention any federal statute of this kind.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following features of the 1918 episode, as described in passage B, most directly illustrates the third of the recurring features identified in passage A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: that reformers had been urging the expansion of state and municipal health departments for more than a decade

choices.label: B
choices.text: that pilot arrangements for the proposed reforms already existed in several cities

choices.label: C
choices.text: that states drew on draft statutes prepared before the outbreak

choices.label: D
choices.text: that after the pandemic subsided, the expanded health departments, reporting requirements, and coordinating bodies remained in place

choices.label: E
choices.text: that full adoption of the reforms had been delayed by budget disputes and local resistance

explanations.correct: Passage A's third feature is that once the emergency recedes, the newly adopted arrangements usually persist. Passage B's final paragraph reports exactly this: the departments did not shrink back, the reporting rules were not repealed, the coordinating bodies continued to meet.
explanations.A: This illustrates the first feature (proposals already in reasonably developed form).
explanations.B: This also supports the first feature (proposals already developed).
explanations.C: This also supports the first feature.
explanations.E: This illustrates the second feature (acceleration pronounced where adoption had been delayed), not the third.

questions.questionStem: The passages most strongly support which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A country that experienced the 1918 pandemic but had no public-health reform proposals in circulation beforehand would likely have emerged from the pandemic with institutional changes comparable to those in the United States.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Had public-health reform proposals not been in circulation in the United States before 1918, the pandemic would probably have produced substantially less institutional change there than it in fact did.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The 1918 pandemic in the United States produced reforms that the reformers of the preceding decade had not anticipated.

choices.label: D
choices.text: American public-health administration before 1918 was already as extensive as the reformers had proposed it should be.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The coordinating bodies established during the pandemic were dismantled once the emergency receded.

explanations.correct: Passage A says outcomes 'reflect what was already available to be accelerated,' and passage B identifies the accelerated reforms with the preexisting reformer program. If nothing comparable had been in circulation, there would have been less for the crisis to accelerate.
explanations.A: This contradicts passage A's claim that outwardly similar outbreaks produce sharply different institutional outcomes, reflecting what was already available to be accelerated.
explanations.C: Passage B treats the reforms as largely those the reformers had been proposing for more than a decade.
explanations.D: Passage B says adoption of the reformers' program had been delayed, not that it was already complete.
explanations.E: Passage B states the coordinating bodies continued to meet after the emergency receded.

questions.questionStem: In passage B, the author's reference to draft statutes that had been prepared before the outbreak functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: suggest that the legislation enacted in 1919 and 1920 was hastily composed and poorly drafted

choices.label: B
choices.text: show that the reforms the pandemic advanced were already in developed form when the pandemic arrived

choices.label: C
choices.text: identify the individual reformers who authored the relevant proposals

choices.label: D
choices.text: illustrate that local authorities had withdrawn their earlier opposition to state-level administration

choices.label: E
choices.text: indicate that the federal government took the lead in drafting public-health legislation during the pandemic

explanations.correct: Passage A's first recurring feature is that the proposals an epidemic advances are typically those already in reasonably developed form. The reference to preexisting draft statutes supplies the factual claim that instantiates this feature for the 1918 episode.
explanations.A: The passage offers no assessment of the drafting quality of the statutes.
explanations.C: The passage does not name any individual reformers.
explanations.D: The passage does not claim local authorities had withdrawn their opposition; it says the pandemic shifted the balance.
explanations.E: The passage attributes the relevant legislation to states, not to the federal government.
